About: Newton's Second Law — F = ma

Source

Lecture
Introductory classical mechanics — Newtonian dynamics (Newton's second law of motion).
Simulation
"Newton's Second Law — F = ma": a single 1-D scene — a steady force on a frictionless car, so a = F/m is the whole story, plus a labeled ⚠ Aristotle counterfactual for contrast.
Concept
Force sets acceleration, not velocity: a = Fnet/m — a steady net force changes v at a steady rate, with no "final speed."
Serves
Live a = Fnet/m readout — same force, double mass ⇒ half acceleration; exact constant-force kinematics (x = ½at² from rest) with balanced mg/N arrows drawn so F is visibly the whole net force.
Inquiry
While F stays on, does v settle at a cruising speed or keep climbing? Same 4 N on 1 kg vs 2 kg — what happens to a? Does x ≈ ½at² near t = 2 s?
Misconception
"A steady push gives a steady speed" — force sets acceleration, not velocity, so a steady push means v keeps climbing at a = Fnet/m.

Force sets acceleration, not speed: a = Fnet/m, fixed while F and m are fixed — so v climbs with no “final speed” in sight. Double m and a halves; double F and it doubles. Explore freely, and open 📊 Data to check x ≈ ½at².

The Physics

Newton’s Second Law — F = ma · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A car sits at rest on a straight road. The sim draws the forces on it and its velocity as arrows, and you set the push F and the mass m.

What you'll learn

  • How to find the net force on the car from the forces acting on it.
  • How the push F and the mass m together decide how the car moves.
  • How the Aristotle model, a rival rule, treats the same push.
A car of mass m at rest. The road pushes up with N, gravity pulls down with mg, F is the applied force along the road, and v is the velocity, drawn as a dot at rest.

What's on screen

  • The car on the road: a side view. The road scrolls past, so the car stays near the left third of the scene.
  • N: the blue arrow up, the normal force from the road.
  • mg: the red arrow down, the weight. Both arrows stop growing at one length, so read their labels for the numbers.
  • F: the amber arrow along the road, 6 px for every newton. It is absent when F = 0.
  • v: the green arrow above the car, with its value. It is a dot when the car is at rest.
  • Flag: a pink flag on the road marks the position x = 8 m.
See itOpen the sim with the car at rest at t = 0, paused. Watch for: the blue N arrow, the red mg arrow, the amber F arrow and the green dot v.

03

The forces on the car are its weight, the normal force and F

Three forces can act on the car. Gravity pulls it down with its weight mg. The road pushes up on it with a normal force N. The slider sets the applied force F, which acts along the road.

The sim always makes N equal to mg, so for m = 4 kg both labels read 39.2 N. These two cancel, which leaves F as the only force along the road. The net force is the vector sum of all the forces on the car:

F⃗net = F⃗1 + F⃗2 + …
Add the forces as vectors. Along one line, add them with their signs.
  • Two forces of +6 N and −2 N along the road add to Fnet = +4 N.
  • Positive means to the right, negative to the left. The road has no friction, so nothing else acts along it.
  • Zero net force is not the same as no forces. mg and N are both present while they cancel.
See itSet the mass to 4 kg and look at the labels. Watch for: N and mg both reading 39.2 N, with F = +4.0 N as the only force along the road.
04

A steady net force gives a steady acceleration

Newton's second law says that the net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration:

F⃗net = m a⃗, so a = Fnet / m
The unit follows: 1 N is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

A force sets the acceleration, not the velocity. While F and m stay fixed, a stays fixed, so the velocity gains the same amount every second and keeps climbing for as long as F acts. From rest, v = a t and x = ½ a t².

With F = +4 N on m = 1 kg, a = 4.00 m/s². At t = 2 s the car has v = 8.00 m/s and x = 8.00 m, which is where the pink flag stands. The acceleration points the way Fnet points, so F = −4 N sends the car left.

For 4 N on 1 kg the line is straight. Its slope is a, and the area under it up to t is the distance x.
See itRun the car with F = +4 N and m = 1 kg until t = 2 s. Watch for: the run pausing at about t = 2 s, with v close to 8 m/s, x close to 8 m and the car at the pink flag.
05

A larger mass gives a smaller acceleration

Since a = Fnet/m, the acceleration grows with the force and shrinks with the mass. Doubling F doubles a, and doubling m halves it. Mass measures how strongly the car resists a change of velocity.

  • 4 N on 1 kg gives a = 4.00 m/s². The same 4 N on 2 kg gives 2.00 m/s², and on 4 kg gives 1.00 m/s².
  • 8 N on 1 kg gives a = 8.00 m/s², twice the 4 N case.
  • On 2 kg at t = 2 s: v = 4.00 m/s and x = 4.00 m, half the values for 1 kg.
F m

These sliders move the sim too.

See itDouble the mass to 2 kg with the same 4 N and run to t = 2 s. Watch for: a = 2.00 m/s², and the run pausing at about t = 2 s with v close to 4 m/s.
06

The Aristotle model makes the velocity follow the force

The ⚠ Aristotle button runs a rival rule that the sim marks as wrong, so that you can watch it fail. In it the velocity is tied to the force:

v = F / k, k = 2 N·s/m, and a = 0
Force sustains a speed. It does not build one up.

With F = +4 N this model gives a steady 2.00 m/s from the first moment, and at +10 N a steady 5.00 m/s. At F = 0 it gives v = 0, so the car stops at once. By t = 2 s it has covered 4.00 m. The Newton model has covered 8.00 m by then, at 8.00 m/s and still speeding up.

The rule feels right because on a real road a steady push does seem to give a steady speed. There friction or drag grows with speed until it cancels the push. Then Fnet is zero and a is zero, as Newton's law says. This road has no such force.

See itSwitch to the Aristotle model with F = +4 N. Watch for: v fixed at 2.00 m/s, the readout a = 0, and the chip ⚠ Aristotle v = F/k at the top left.
07

Where it matters

  • Cars. A 1200 kg car with a net force of 3600 N along the road accelerates at 3.0 m/s². At that rate it needs about 9.3 s to reach 100 km/h.
  • Loaded and empty. The same engine force on a loaded truck of twice the mass gives half the acceleration. This is why heavy vehicles are slow to speed up and slow to stop.
  • Falling rain. A raindrop speeds up until air drag equals its weight. The net force is then zero, so the speed stays steady. A steady speed means a = 0, and it does not mean there is no force.
08

Summary

In one line. Newton's second law ties the net force on a body to its mass and its motion.

Key points

  • F⃗net = m a⃗, so a = Fnet/m. Force sets the acceleration, and the velocity keeps changing while F acts.
  • Double F and a doubles. Double m and a halves.
  • From rest with fixed F and m: v = a t and x = ½ a t². The Aristotle rule v = F/k fails because it ignores hidden friction.

Common mix-ups

  • "A steady push gives a steady speed." It gives a steady acceleration. The speed keeps climbing.
  • "A bigger force means a bigger velocity." A bigger force means a bigger acceleration.
  • "The net force is the force I apply." It is the sum of all forces. Here mg and N cancel, so only F is left.

Things to try on your own

  • Set F = +8 N and m = 2 kg, and predict a from F/m before you read it.
  • Set F = −4 N and see which way the car moves and faces.
  • Compare x at t = 2 s for 4 N on 1 kg in the Newton and Aristotle models.
